title: Health rebate cut a stitch-up, says Taylor
full_text:
Health Minister Mark Butler is reducing private health insurance rebates for older Australians and possibly pushing thousands off the system because he says there is no “lazy free money”, as the sector takes its case to stop the reforms directly to Anthony Albanese.
The opposition stepped up its criticism of the federal government’s move to remove the higher rate of over-65s rebate for private health insurance, with Angus Taylor accusing it of shifting costs to state health departments. The Australian revealed on Thursday that state health ministers were rebelling against the federal government over the surprise change.
“We absolutely oppose what the government is doing on this,” the Opposition Leader said. “And we want to make sure that older Australians have the private health insurance that they deserve. We don’t want to see them leaving private health insurance.
“We’re now seeing state health ministers say what we’ve known for some time, which is this is just a cost-shifting exercise. This is a cost-shifting exercise where the Health Minister is shifting costs to state governments.” Opposition deputy leader Jane Hume said the government’s changes amounted to a “mean-spirited $11bn tax on older Australians”. “They’ve done the right thing for years, they’ve alleviated the pressure on the public system, and now you’re going to tax them more,” she told Channel 7.
Mr Butler on Friday defended the budget changes, saying they would help fund more aged-care services and that it built up intergenerational equity, meaning that people on the same income would get the same rebate regardless of their age. “There’s no lazy, free money lying around … We have to take sometimes quite hard decisions in a budget,” he said.
“We’ve had to find more money to fund aged-care services. We’ve put an eye-watering amount of extra money into aged care over the last few years to get it out of the position that the royal commission described as neglect, and to fund the extra demand that’s coming from the ageing of the Baby Boomer generation.
“I think this has been a difficult decision. Of course I’d prefer not to make it, but I think it takes us back to the old position where people received health insurance subsidies based on their income rather than their age.” Mr Butler has also cited intergenerational equity as a key reason for making private health rebates the same for all ages. But the latest official figures from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare showed the dramatic imbalance in public health spending by age group, with $44.7m in taxpayer funds spent on every 1000 people 85 and over in 2023-24, compared with $7.4m on every 1000 people in the 25-29 group.
In a letter to the Prime Minister in June from peak groups such as National Seniors Australia, Patients Australia, the Australian Medical Association, the eight group chiefs highlighted the disproportionate impact the measure would likely have on lower-income and regional Australians.
“The academic literature the department itself cites … finds that lower-income older Australians are several times most price-responsive than the cohort average. The policy treats all over-65s identically,” the letter says. “The change will also impact the government’s efforts to improve access to the public hospital system … more older people will end up in public hospitals and this will simply increase pressure on an already stretched system.” Economists were split on the system. Alastair Furnival, partner at Evaluate Consultancy and a former staffer to Coalition ageing ministers, said there was a valid aim to subsiding older people in private health insurance.
“A lot of what happens in the private sector is also preventive,” he said. “And so it’s just a very efficient thing to invest in. It saves you all that money down the line.
“Older people need more healthcare. So even if you spend slightly more, it’s probably an efficient thing to do.” But University of Melbourne professorial fellow Yuting Zhang said the move to remove the rebate was supported by research.
The broader issue that limited capacity in both the private and public healthcare systems, she said, was the amount of time surgeons and medical professionals had. “If there is more time in the private system, that means they have less time in the public system,” she said. “So it really doesn’t reduce waiting time in the public system, more people using private system.”
